name: Mortis-Arida

civilization.name: The Aridan Builders
civilization.notes: A civilization that attempted to terraform their dying world by building massive atmospheric processors. They failed, and their machines stand as monuments to a desperate gamble against planetary decay.

specific_features: Massive atmospheric processor towers still partially operational
description: Mortis-Arida is a world that almost survived, its surface bearing the marks of a civilization's desperate attempt to reverse the death of their planet through industrial-scale intervention. The dried ocean beds stretch across the equatorial regions, their floors cracked into tessellated patterns beneath a thin layer of dust that the wind redistributes in an endless, pointless cycle. The canal systems that once carried water from pole to equator are now dry channels of dust and rubble, their engineering still impressive even in ruin, straight lines scored across the landscape with a precision that speaks of organized will.

The thin atmosphere tastes of dust and chemicals, residues from the atmospheric processors that still operate at reduced capacity in their towers scattered across the highlands. These machines were designed to thicken the atmosphere and restore conditions suitable for life, but they were built too late and too few, their output insufficient to overcome the rate of atmospheric loss. They stand as monuments to industrial ambition, towers of metal and ceramic reaching hundreds of meters into the sky, their intake vents still drawing thin air and processing it through filters clogged with centuries of dust.

The Aridan Builders left extensive records in their archive structures, climate models and engineering documents that show they understood their situation with scientific precision. They knew the atmosphere was thinning, they calculated the timeline, and they launched a terraforming program with every resource their industrial civilization could muster. The math never worked, the energy requirements exceeded their capabilities by an order of magnitude, but they built anyway, choosing action over acceptance. Their population declined in parallel with their atmosphere, each generation smaller and more dispersed, until the last entries in the archives were written by individuals who knew they were the end.

The partially operational atmospheric processors continue to run on geothermal power, their autonomous systems maintaining themselves with dwindling efficiency. Some analysts argue they should be shut down as a mercy, ending a purpose that can never be fulfilled. Others propose upgrading them with modern technology to finish what the Builders started, a project that would take decades but could potentially restore the planet to habitability. The debate is as much philosophical as practical: does humanity have an obligation to complete the work of an extinct civilization, and would the Builders have wanted their world inherited by strangers?
